claims.text: Rapid, spatially uniform heating causes all metal precursors to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Synchronous reduction kinetically traps the metals in a single-phase, homogeneous alloy.
Synchronous reduction prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
The proposed starting material is a mixture of noble-metal precursors dispersed on a support or in solution.
Minimizing temperature gradients and using a sufficiently high heating rate prevents sequential reduction and nucleation.
Synchronized surface-energy minimization during initial nucleation locks the atoms into a high-entropy alloy arrangement.
Rapid, uniform reduction decreases local concentration fluctuations.
Simultaneous nucleation traps the constituent metals in a mixed state before elemental diffusion can produce segregation.
Uniform heating will produce nanoparticles with a nearly homogeneous atomic distribution, minimal elemental segregation, and a single crystalline phase.
Slower or spatially non-uniform heating will produce more phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity than uniform heating.
Slower or non-uniform heating permits sequential reduction and nucleation.
The mechanism should apply reliably to rapidly synthesized noble-metal systems whose precursors have closely matched reduction potentials.
The mechanism may fail when reduction kinetics or precursor stabilities differ substantially.
The mechanism may fail in non-noble-metal systems where other factors dominate nucleation.
Precursor chemistry, including ligand interactions and solubility, may modify the effect of thermal uniformity.
The controlled comparison changes thermal uniformity while holding all other factors constant.
Failure of uniform heating to improve alloy homogeneity relative to the non-uniform-heating control would falsify the hypothesis.
